cover: This talk is about typing promise resolution in the SKJS verifier: contracts for native promises, a sound generic Awaited type, and where TypeScript's own Awaited is unsound. The generic part is partly supported, and the forms it does not yet cover are recorded as gaps.
outline: There are five parts. First, the problem: generic forwarding has no sound type. Second, TypeScript's Awaited, and why it is unsound. Third, contracts for native promises. Fourth, generic Awaited of T, through qualified binders. And fifth, the results: target programs, the census of the corpus, and the limits that remain.
problem: Here is the problem. The function wrap takes a value x of any type T and returns it from an async function, promising a Promise of Awaited of T. On the base branch, the verifier cannot check this. Its two trusted contracts, for await and for async return, only allow primitives on the non-promise side. But T may be a promise or an object, and no type says what x becomes once a promise resolves with it. So wrap is refused.
types: Five definitions. Prim is the primitives, and Obj everything else. A thenable is an object with a callable then. Resolution fulfills a promise directly with a primitive or a non-thenable, and calls a thenable's then. Promise of B is a native promise whose fulfillment values lie in B. And N is the set of values that can never have a callable then.
awaited: TypeScript already has an answer: the Awaited type. It is a conditional type. Null and undefined map to themselves. An object type that declares a then method is unwrapped recursively through the first parameter of its callback. Everything else, including object types with no declared then, maps to itself. Crucially, all of this is decided from the declared type.
unsound: That is unsound, because object types are open. In the first example, a record with a hidden then method is passed as a plain record of type n number. TypeScript says the awaited value is that record, but Node delivers the string hi. In the second example, an object acquires a then method after a promise has fulfilled with it. Awaiting the promise gives the object, and awaiting the object again gives 42, while TypeScript claims both are the record type. So resolution is not idempotent.
twice: There is a second problem, which any design must face: resolution can happen twice. Here a promise fulfills with an object, and the object acquires a then method afterwards. Await, Promise dot resolve, and Promise dot all read the fulfillment value once, and give back the original object. But an async return, then, catch, finally, and the Promise constructor all resolve a fresh promise with that value, and so they call the new then, and produce 42. So observing a fulfillment value is safe at any payload, while resolving it again is safe only if the payload stays non-thenable.
native: That leads to the native promise contracts. A Promise of B is a native promise with stable standard behaviour. Await observes, so it admits a promise of any payload T, and a value in N, the stable non-thenables, at its own type. Async return, Promise dot resolve of a plain value, catch and finally resolve again, so they require their payloads to lie in N. Promise dot resolve of an existing native promise returns that promise itself, so it admits any payload.
qualified: Now the generic case. When a signature mentions Awaited of T, that mention implies a bound on T, as if it had been written there: T is resolvable. Bounds are read off the signature, never off the body. Resolvable means that T has a classification, which fixes two associated types: T's observed type, what await yields, and T's result type, what a fresh resolution yields, which is never thenable. Awaited of T is T's result type. So wrap reads as: for every resolvable T, a function from T to a promise of T's result. This is not a subtype bound: it leaves the values of T alone, and each call supplies the classification of its type argument. There is one other implied bound: a promise argument of an imported or library signature implies that T is a stable non-thenable.
rules: So who fixes the observed and result types? Four rules classify a type argument. A stable type is its own observed and result type. A native promise of A is observed as A, and its result is A's result. A union is classified arm by arm. And a subtype may take its supertype's classification. The producer proposes a classification for each call, and Lean checks it and computes the two types from it. Inside a body they stay abstract: the result is never thenable, and the observed type resolves to the result. The narrowing rule has a consequence: number can be classified with result number or string. So the result is not unique, and Awaited corresponds to the least one.
compare: Comparing TypeScript's Awaited with the least result type. On primitives they agree. On a promise of number, and on a promise of a promise of number, both give number. On a union of a number and a promise of a readonly string array, both give number or readonly string array. On an open record, Awaited gives the record, which is unsound, while there is no classification, so the program is refused. The same holds for PromiseLike. In short, the least result type agrees with Awaited wherever the result stays non-thenable, and refuses where Awaited is unsound.
targets: Here is where the target programs stand. Parameters and mutable cells of Awaited of T, and the numeric instance of wrap, verify end to end. The generic wrap with return await is a recorded gap: resolution inside a qualified body is refused. The number-bounded function back is also a gap, because of the non-uniqueness we just saw. The open record, the erasure to Promise of unknown, and forwarding a promise of a record, the 42 case, are all refused. Overall, all 888 pipeline cases meet their expected outcome, and eleven generic promise cases are recorded as gaps.
census: On the SKJS corpus, before this work, SKJS accepts 2674 units, of which the verifier verifies 2466, and six remain unverified for promise reasons. With this work, the one that awaits an array now verifies, since an array is a stable value. The two that await a PromiseLike are unchanged, since they need a rule for typed thenables. The two that return a fresh object from an async function are not yet measured, and the last one is an unrelated restriction on keys of a Promise type.
limits: Finally, the limits that remain. Await and return inside generic bodies, proof search for qualified binders, and higher-order uses remain open. Awaited of T is not unique, so a result bounded by T needs a decision, such as taking the least result. Awaiting a PromiseLike needs a rule for its typed then method. Further rules would extend coverage: returning a fresh object, the values a Promise executor resolves, a second reaction on an already-settled promise, thenables that only resolve to themselves, and promises that can never fulfill. And there are gaps already listed: an explicit catch of string, source copies of promises, reactions on Promise of void, and publishing a named generic wrapper. Thank you.
